11:2: And there shall dwell upon him the spirit of prophecy from before the Lord: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord.
11:3: He shall bring him to the fear of the Lord: and he shall not judge according to the sight of His eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears.
11:4: But with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and reprove with faithfulness the needy of the earth; and he shall smite the sinners of the earth with the word of his mouth, and with the speech of His lips he shall slay Armillus the wicked.
11:5: And the righteous shall be round about him, and the workers of faith shall draw nigh unto him.
11:6: In the days of the Messiah of Israel peace shall be multiplied in the earth. The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall dwell with the kid; and the calf, and the lion, and the fatling together; and a little sucking child shall be leading them.
11:7: And the cow and the bear shall feed together, their young ones shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox.
11:8: And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put forth his hand on the sight of the pupil of the eyes of the cockatrice.
11:9: They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the fear of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
11:10: And there shall be at that time a son of the son of Jesse, who shall stand for an ensign of the people; kings shall obey him, and the place of his dwelling shall be in glory.
11:11: And it shall come to pass at that time, that the Lord shall add a second time His might to redeem the remnant of His people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pattros, and from India, and from Elam, and from Babylon, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.
11:12: And He shall lift up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the scattered of Israel, and the captivity of Judah He shall gather together from the four winds of the earth.
11:13: The envy of the house of Ephraim shall depart, and those that oppress the house of Judah shall come to an end: those of the house of Ephraim shall not envy the house of Judah; and those of the house of Judah shall not oppress the house of Ephraim.
11:14: They shall be united in one mind to smite the Philistines towards the west: they shall spoil the children of the east. Against Edom and Moab they shall stretch out their hands, and the children of Ammon shall obey them.
11:15: And the Lord shall dry up the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and shall lift the stroke of His strength upon Euphrates by the word of His prophets, and shall smite it in seven streams, and men shall walk through it dryshod.
11:16: And there shall be a paved way for the remnant of His people, which shall be left, from Assyria, like as it was to Israel in the day of their coming up from the land of Egypt.
12:1: And thou shalt say at that time, I will confess before Thee, O Lord, for that I have sinned before Thee, Thine anger is upon me; but when I return to the law, Thine anger will turn from me, and Thou wilt have mercy on me.
12:2: Behold, in the word of God is my salvation; I am trusting, and shall not be moved, because my strength and my praise is the fear of the Lord: He hath spoken by His word, and He is become my salvation.
12:3: And ye shall receive a new doctrine with joy from the chosen of the righteous.
12:4: And at that time shall ye say, Praise before the Lord, pray in His name, declare His doings among the people, remember ye that powerful is His name.
12:5: Praise the Lord, for He has done mighty works; this is revealed in all the earth.

13:1: The Burden Of The Cup Of Cursing To Give To Babylon To Drink, Which Isaiah The Son Of Amoz Did Prophesy.
13:2: Against the fortified city that dwells securely lift up the ensign, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the nobles.
13:3: I have commanded those that are prepared by me, I have also called together my mighty ones, that they may avenge my wrath upon them, my strength, and my praise.
13:4: There is a voice of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people: the voice of the tumultuous assembly of kings, of nations being assembled, the Lord of hosts is mustering the armies for battle.
13:5: They are coming from a far country, from the ends of the earth: the Lord and the vessels of the cup of cursing before Him, to destroy all the wicked of the earth.
13:6: Howl ye, for nigh is the day, ready to come from before the Lord; like spoil from before the Almighty it shall come.
13:7: Therefore shall all hands be slackened, and every man's heart shall melt.
13:8: They shall be struck with consternation; distress and pangs shall take hold of them; they shall tremble as with the trembling of a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their countenances shall be like flames of fire.
13:9: Behold, the day from before the presence of the Lord cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and He shall destroy the sinners out of it.
13:10: For the stars of heaven and their constellations shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth; and the moon shall not cause her light to shine.
13:11: And I will visit the inhabitants of the world with the punishment for evil, and the wicked for their iniquity: and I will put an end to the greatness of the wicked, and the strength of the mighty I will humble.
13:12: And I will love them that fear me more than gold, in which the sons of men glory; and those that keep the law more than the fine gold of Ophir.
13:13: Therefore I will shake the heavens, and the earth shall remove out of her place, from before the presence of the Lord of hosts, and in the day of the fierceness of His anger.
13:14: And he shall be as a roe chased, and as sheep when there is none to gather them together: they shall every man turn to his own people, and flee every one into his own land.
13:15: Every one that shall be found in her shall be slain, and every one that shall enter into the fortified cities shall be slain by the sword.
13:16: And their children shall be dashed before their eyes; their houses shall be plundered, and their wives ravished.
13:17: Behold, I am bringing upon them the Medes, who are not impelled by silver; and as for gold, they delight not in it.
13:18: And their bows shall strike through the young men; and they shall not compassionate the child of the womb; their eye shall not spare the children.
13:19: And Babylon shall become, she that was aforetimes the joy of kings, the beauty of the Chaldeens' excellency, as the overthrow wherewith the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.
13:20: It shall not be inhabited for ever; nor shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch his tent there, neither shall the shepherds dwell there.
13:21: But the martens shall lodge there; and their houses shall be filled with owls; and there shall the ostriches dwell; and devils shall delight themselves there.
13:22: The wild cats shall shriek in their palaces; and dragons in the place of the abodes of their luxuries. And nigh to come is the time of the destruction of Babylon, and her days shall not be prolonged.
14:1: For the Lord will have compassion upon the house of Jacob, and will delight again in Israel, and shall make them to dwell in their land; and proselytes shall be joined unto them, and they shall be united unto the house of Jacob.

14:4: That thou shalt take up this proverb against the king of Babylon, and say, How hath the dominion that made us servile ceased! How is come to an end the strength of the sinner!
14:5: The Lord hath broken the strength of the wicked, the government of sinners,
14:6: Of him who was smiting the people in fury, with a perpetual stroke, of him who was ruling the nations in anger, ruling and none hindered.
14:7: The whole earth is at rest, is quiet, they rejoice with a song.
14:8: Rulers also rejoiced over thee; the rich in treasures said, Since thou art laid down, the destroyer is not come up upon us.
14:9: Hell from beneath is moved for thee, to meet thee at thy coming; she rouseth for thee the mighty: all the rich in treasures, all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones.
14:10: All of them shall answer and say unto thee, Art thou become sick as we? Unto us, thou hast become like.
14:11: Thy glory is brought down to the grave, the rattling noise of the songs of the musical instruments: the worm is spread under thee, and upon thee vermin.
14:12: How art thou cast down from on high, who wast shining among the sons of men as the star Venus among the stars: thou art dashed down to the earth, who wast a slaughterer among the nations.
14:13: And thou, thou hast said in thy heart, I will climb up the heavens; I will place the throne of my kingdom above the people of God, and I will sit upon the mountain of the solemn assembly upon the ends of the north;
14:14: I will ascend over all people; I will be higher than all of them.
14:15: But to the grave thou shalt be brought down, to the ends of the pit of the place of perdition.
14:16: Those that see thee shall look attentively at thee, they shall consider thee, and say, "Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that laid waste kingdoms?
14:17: That made the world as a wilderness, that laid waste its cities, and did not open the gate to his prisoners?
14:18: All the kings of the nations, all of them, lie down in glory, each in his eternal abode."
14:19: But thou art cast out of thy grave as a hidden branch, as those hidden among the slain, as those pierced by the sword, as those that are descending the lowest pit of the place of destruction, as a carcass trodden under foot.
14:20: Thou shalt not be like one of them in burial; because thou hast destroyed thy country, thou hast slain thy people: the seed of evildoers shall not be established for ever.
14:21: Prepare ye slaughter for his children, for the iniquity of their fathers; lest they rise and possess the earth, and the faces of the world be filled with enemies.

14:25: To break the Assyrian in my land, and upon the mountains of my people I will tread him under foot; then there shall depart from them his dominion, and his yoke off from their necks shall cease.
14:26: This is the purpose that is purposed upon all the inhabitants of the earth; and this is the might of the ruler which is lifted up over all the kingdoms.
14:27: For the Lord of hosts has purposed, and who can remove it? yea, His power is exalted, and who can withstand it?

15:6: For the waters of Nimrim shall become desolate; for the herbage is withered away; the grass faileth, there is no green herb.
15:7: Therefore the remnant of their riches, shall be plundered; and their border, which is by the western sea, shall be taken from them.
15:8: For the cry encompasses the border of Moab; unto Eglaim are they howling, and unto Beer Elim they are crying aloud.

16:1: They shall bring tributes to the Messiah of Israel, who shall prevail over those who are in the wilderness, unto the mountain of the congregation of Zion.
16:2: Otherwise it shall come to pass, as a bird which men have driven away, being cast out of its nest, the daughters of Moab shall be led round about, made to Wadi Arnon.
16:3: Take counsel, execute counsel. Make thy shadow as the night in the day, in the midst of the noonday: hide the outcasts; touch not the dispersed.
16:4: Let my outcasts dwell with thee, O kingdom of Moab! be thou a covert to them on account of the spoilers: for the extortioner is at an end, the spoiler ceaseth, all that trampled under foot have come to au end.
16:5: Then the throne of the Messiah of Israel shall be established in goodness, and he shall sit upon it in truth in the city of David, judging and seeking justice, and executing truth.

16:7: Therefore the Moabites shall howl: over the Moabites all of them shall cry aloud; and they shall howl over the men of the city of their strength; they, mourning, shall say, surely they are conquered.
16:8: Because the armies of Heshbon are spoiled, the multitude of Sebama are killed, the kings of the people have killed their rulers; they reached unto Jazer; they strayed to the desert; their outcasts passed by, they crossed the sea.
16:9: Therefore, as I have brought armies against Jazer, so will I bring slayers against Sibmah; I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh! for upon thy harvest, and upon thy vintage the robbers have fallen.
16:10: And joy is taken away and gladness out of the fruitful field, and in the vineyards they shall not rejoice, neither shall they play sport; in the vats the treaders shall not tread out the wine; the treading of grapes I have made to cease.
16:11: Wherefore the bowels of the Moabites shall sound as a harp, and their heart shall mourn over the men of the city of their strength.
16:12: And it shall come to pass, that one shall see, that when Moab is wearied out upon his high place, he shall enter his idol-temple to pray, yet he shall not prevail.
16:13: This is the word which the Lord spake concerning the Moabites long ago:
16:14: But now the Lord hath spoken, saying: Within three years, as the years of an hireling, the glory of the Moabites shall come to an end, with all that great multitude; and the remnant shall be small, a few; all their glory shall come to an end.
17:1: The Burden Of The Cup Of Cursing To Give Damascus To Drink. Behold, Damascus is removed, so as to be no more a kingdom: and it shall be as a city laid waste.
17:2: Their cities are deserted, they are laid waste; they shall be for dwelling-places for flocks of sheep; they shall lie down, and none shall make them to move away.
17:3: The government shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of the solitary ones from Syria, and their glory shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, saith the Lord of hosts.
17:4: And it shall come to pass at that time, that the glory of Jacob shall be humbled, and the riches of his glory shall be carried away.
17:5: And it shall be, as when one gathereth the standing harvest, and reapeth the ears with his arm; and it shall be as one that is gathering ears in the valley of giants.
17:6: Yet a gleaning shall be left in it, as in the shaking of the olive tree, two or three berries on the top of the uppermost branch; so shall the righteous be left lonely in the midst of the world, among the kingdoms, saith the Lord, the God of Israel.
17:7: At that time a man shall stay himself upon the service of his Maker, and his eyes shall hopefully look for the WORD, the Holy One of Israel.
17:8: He shall not rest upon the altars, the work of his hands, or stay himself upon that which his fingers have prepared, neither upon the groves nor upon the sun-images.
17:9: At that time the cities of their strength shall be as a fortification that was laid desolate and waste from before the children of Israel, and each shall be a desolation.
17:10: Because thou hast forsaken the God of thy salvation, and thou hast not remembered the fear of the Mighty One, whose Word was thy support; therefore thou hast planted a choice plant, and hast multiplied despicable works.
17:11: After that ye were sanctified to be a people, there ye made your works despicable; and also when ye came to the land, the place of my Shekinah, there it was your duty' to worship me; ye forsook my worship, and ye served idols: ye abhorred repentance till the day of your destruction came, then your sorrow was a breathing out of soul.
17:12: Woe to the multitude of many people, which make a noise like the noise of the sea, and to the tumultuous assembly of kings, which roar like the roaring of mighty waters.

18:3: All ye inhabitants of the world, and ye dwellers on the earth, when the standard is lifted up on the mountains, ye shall see the standard, and the trumpet shall sound, ye shall hear of redemption.

18:6: They shall be left together unto the fowl of the mountains, and to the beasts of the earth: all the fowls of the heavens shall dwell upon them in the summer, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon them.
18:7: At that time shall one bring an offering unto the Lord of hosts, to a people oppressed and spoiled, to a people that was mighty in times past, and shall be so in time to come, a people oppressed and robbed, whose land the nations have spoiled, unto the place which is called by the name of the Lord of hosts, whose Shekinah is in the mountain of Zion.
19:1: The Burden Of The Cup Of Cursing To Make The Egyptians To Drink. Behold, the Lord is revealed in the cloud of His glory, to take vengeance of the Egyptians; and the idols of the Egyptians shall be broken before His face, and the heart of the Egyptians shall be melted within them.
19:2: And I will excite Egyptians against Egyptians, and they shall wage war, every man against his brother, and every man against his neighbour: city against city, kingdom against kingdom.
19:3: And the spirit of the Egyptians shall melt within them, and their wise men I will destroy: and they shall seek to the idols, and to the charmers, to the deceitful, and to the diviners.
19:4: And I will deliver the Egyptians into the hand of a cruel lord; and a fierce king shall rule over them, saith the Lord of the world, the Lord of hosts.
19:5: And the waters of the sea shall be laid desolate, and their river shall be wasted and dried up.
19:6: And their rivers shall be laid waste, and their deep streams shall be dried up and wasted: the reeds and flags shall not grow.
19:7: And the greatest part of the river shall wither, and that which is on its bank, and every sown place of their rivers shall wither, and shall be dried up, and nothing shall grow.
19:8: The fishermen shall be laid desolate, and all they that cast angle into the brook, and they that spread nets upon the faces of the waters shall be destroyed.
19:9: They shall be confounded which work combed flax, and weave nets of it.
19:10: And there shall be trodden under foot the well watered place, where they have been making pits, waterpools each for himself.
19:11: Surely the princes of Tanes have become foolish; the wise, the counsellors of Pharaoh have counselled an erroneous counsel; how will Pharaoh, We are the sons of the wise, and thou art the son of ancient kings.
19:12: Where are thy wise men? Let them tell thee now, and let them know what the Lord of hosts has counselled against Egypt.
19:13: The princes of Tanes have become foolish, the men of Memphis have erred; they caused the Egyptians, the lords of the provinces, to err.
19:14: The Lord hath sent among them a spirit of error, and they have caused the Egyptians to err in all their works, as a drunkard staggereth, and tramples in his vomit.
19:15: And the Egyptians shall have no king to reign, no prince, noble, governor, or ruler.
19:16: At that time the Egyptians shall be weak, they shall be afraid, and fear on account of the exultation of the power of the Lord of hosts, which He is lifting up against them.
19:17: And the land of the house of Judah shall be a terror unto Egypt; if anyone mention it unto them, they shall tremble because of the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he hath counselled against them.
19:18: At that time, there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt, speaking the language of Canaan, and swearing by the name of the Lord of hosts. The city of Beth-Shemesh, which is to be destroyed, shall be called one of them.
19:19: At that time there shall be prepared an altar before the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt; and a pillar by the border thereof before the Lord.
19:20: And it shall be for a sign, and for a witness before the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt, when they shall pray before the Lord because of their oppressors, and He shall send unto them a Saviour, and a Judge, and He shall deliver them.
19:21: And the power of the Lord shall be revealed to do good to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians shall know the fear of the Lord at that time, and they shall worship with holy sacrifices and offerings; yea, they shall vow vows before the Lord, and shall perform them.
19:22: And the Lord shall smite Egypt with a stroke, and shall heal them, and they shall return to the worship of the Lord, and He shall hear their prayers, and shall heal them.
19:23: And at that time there shall be a highway from Egypt to Assyria; and the Assyrians shall fight against the Egyptians, and the Egyptians against the Assyrians, and the Egyptians shall serve the Assyrians.
19:24: And at that time Israel shall be a third party to the Egyptians and to the Assyrians, a blessing in the midst of the land.
19:25: Whom the Lord of hosts hath blessed, saying, Blessed be my people, whom I have brought out of Egypt; and because they sinned before me, I carried them captive into Assyria, but when they repent, they are called my people, and Israel mine inheritance.

n: These prophecies occurred when Assyria rose to power. Syria and Israel formed an alliance against Judah ({{Isaiah 7:1-2|Isaiah 7:1–2}}; see {{2 Kings 16:5|2 Kings 16:5}}). God used Assyria as a tool to punish Syria, Israel, and Judah ({{Isaiah 7:1-10:34|Isaiah 7–10}}).
In this long section of the book, the nation of Israel was confronted with a vision of God, similar to how Isaiah was confronted in {{Isaiah 6:1-13|chapter 6}}.

The judgement messages in these chapters are against Jacob’s people and against Assyria. Jacob’s people included the northern kingdom. The northern kingdom was also called Israel and Ephraim. Jacob’s people included the southern kingdom as well. The southern kingdom was also called Judah. God was very angry with his people because they were proud.

The prophets, judges and kings didn’t follow God’s instructions for leaders. These instructions were recorded in Deuteronomy 13:1–5 and Deuteronomy 17:8–20. The leaders made laws that were unfair and they took away people’s rights. God used the Assyrian army as his tool to bring judgement against his people. That is how Assyria was the war club that carried out God’s anger. But Assyria’s king didn’t recognise that he had success in battles because God allowed him to. He was proud. He claimed that his own power and strength made him successful. That is why God would bring judgement against Assyria as well.

The messages of hope in these chapters are about a ruler and king who wasn’t proud. In chapter 9, Isaiah prophesied about a child from David’s family line. This child would become a ruler who did what was fair and right. His rule would last for ever. He would be called Wonderful Adviser and Mighty God. He would be called Father Who Lives For Ever and Prince Who Brings Peace.

In chapter 11, Isaiah prophesied again about this ruler. He was called a Branch like the Branch of the Lord in Isaiah 4:2. He would rule with the help of the Spirit of the Lord. That is another name for the Holy Spirit. Life in the kingdom of this ruler would be very different. It wouldn’t be like life in the world that people were used to. Everyone everywhere on earth would know who God is and would serve him. No one and nothing would cause harm to anyone or anything. Isaiah described this by talking about how children would play with animals that are usually dangerous. No harm would come to them. This was a picture of the peace that this ruler would bring.

Jews came to understand these messages of hope as prophecies about the messiah. New Testament writers came to understand them as prophecies about Jesus. Isaiah wrote out songs of praise that God’s people would sing one day. They would sing them after God finished bringing judgement against them. They would sing them once God brought them comfort. Isaiah chapters 40 to 66 talk about this comfort. In the songs in chapter 12 the Israelites recognise that God is their Saviour. They tell everyone about him. They help all nations on earth know God and honour him. These joyful songs celebrate God as the Holy One of Israel.

{{Isaiah 9:8-10:4|Isaiah 9:8–10:4}} shows that the Lord’s moral law is supreme. This means God’s standards of right and wrong stand above every nation and ruler. The next section explains what this truth means: 

- Assyria was only a tool in God’s hands. Because of this, Assyria was also responsible to God. Like every other nation, it would face judgment for its sin ({{Isaiah 10:5-19|Isaiah 10:5–19}}, {{Isaiah 10:28-34|28–34}}).

- Those among God’s people who trusted in him and obeyed his covenant would be rescued ({{Isaiah 10:20-27|Isaiah 10:20–27}}).

- God would establish his kingdom on earth ({{Isaiah 11:1-16|Isaiah 11}}).

*shoot … stump … Branch from his roots*: This new growth represents the continuation of David's royal family line, even after it almost ended during the exile in Babylon (see also {{Isaiah 6:13|Isaiah 6:13}}; {{Isaiah 39:7|39:7}}; {{Revelation 22:16|Rev 22:16}}). This new growth from the old roots will not resemble the previous weak and unjust descendants of David (see {{Isaiah 4:2|Isaiah 4:2}}). Jesus, the Messiah (God's chosen one), is the final fulfillment.

- justice and righteousness ({{Isaiah 11:4|Isaiah 11:4}}), 

- peace ({{Isaiah 11:8|Isaiah 11:8}}), and 

- the extension of God's kingdom to all nations ({{Isaiah 11:10|Isaiah 11:10}}; see also {{Isaiah 32:15-16|32:15–16}}). 

- The promised Messiah will have great wisdom and understanding, like King Solomon. He will also have knowledge and reverence for the Lord ({{1 Kings 3:28|1 Kings 3:28}}; {{1 Kings 4:29|4:29}}; {{Proverbs 1:1-7|Proverbs 1:1–7}}; {{Proverbs 2:6-7|2:6–7}}). 

- The *Spirit of counsel and strength* refers to {{Isaiah 9:6|Isaiah 9:6}}. The Messiah will be wise and have the power to rule righteously.

*the fear of the LORD*: This means having deep respect and reverence for the Lord. It does not mean being afraid in a frightened way (see also {{Isaiah 11:2|Isaiah 11:2}} and {{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}).

- The poor and the exploited would receive the justice due to them, which the wicked leaders of Judah had previously withheld. 

- *the rod of his mouth*: See {{Psalm 2:9|Psalm 2:9}}; {{Revelation 19:15|Revelation 19:15}}.

Because the Messiah is righteous in his character, his rule will show justice, righteousness, and truth. These qualities will mark his reign.

This will be very different from the condition of Jerusalem described in {{Isaiah 1:21|Isaiah 1:21}}. There, the city is described as unjust and unfaithful.
This prophecy was partly fulfilled during Isaiah's time or soon after. The complete fulfillment will occur when the Messiah (God's chosen one) arrives to begin and fully establish the age to come.
*neither harm nor destroy*: There will be no wrongdoers, corruption, or sin on God's holy mountain (Zion).

- *the Root of Jesse*: See {{Isaiah 11:1|Isaiah 11:1}}; {{Revelation 5:5|Revelation 5:5}}; {{Revelation 22:16|22:16}}. 

- The Messiah will bring salvation to the entire world ({{Isaiah 2:1-5|Isaiah 2:1–5}}). People from other nations will serve as priests and Levites ({{Isaiah 66:20-21|Isaiah 66:20–21}}), but only if they repent and believe in the true God.

- The first time the Lord reached out his hand was during the exodus. The second time will be in the future when the Messiah gathers non-Jewish people ({{Isaiah 11:10|Isaiah 11:10}}) and his own people living among them ({{Isaiah 11:11|11:11}}). 

The exodus remained a symbol of hope for those in exile (see {{Isaiah 11:16|Isaiah 11:16}}; {{Isaiah 35:8|35:8}}; {{Isaiah 40:3|40:3}}; {{Isaiah 43:19-20|43:19–20}}; {{Isaiah 48:21|48:21}}). 

- The remnant of his people included Israelites who survived the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions and were exiled.

*jealousy of Ephraim … and … Judah*: The two kingdoms became enemies during Judah's war with the alliance of Syria and Israel (see {{Isaiah 7:1-12|Isaiah 7:1–12}}). In the future, they would work together in military missions.

- *the Philistines to the west*: The Philistines were Israel’s historic enemy. 

- The nations to the east included the Edomites, Moabites, and Ammonites. All these enemies would be defeated.

Isaiah used images from Israel's past exodus to encourage his listeners. He promised that God would lead his people out of Assyria just as he led them out of Egypt ({{Exodus 14:29-15:18|Exodus 14:29–15:18}}; see also {{Revelation 16:12|Revelation 16:12}}).
God's comfort is the main topic of {{Isaiah 40:1-66:24|Isaiah 40–66}}.

The prophet's personal song of praise for God's salvation concludes the reflections on trust in {{Isaiah 7:1-12:6|Isaiah 7–12}}. God will show he is trustworthy in his promises to rescue his people, even though they initially refused to trust him. The song anticipates {{Isaiah 40:1-66:24|Isaiah 40–66}} with its themes of: 

- salvation,

- forgiveness,

- praise,

- joy, and

- the nations.

- God's promise to save includes:

- reconciliation ({{Isaiah 1:18|Isaiah 1:18}}),

- participation ({{Isaiah 11:10|Isaiah 11:10}}),

- cleansing and protection ({{Isaiah 4:3-6|Isaiah 4:3–6}}),

- peace and confidence ({{Isaiah 32:16-17|Isaiah 32:16–17}}), and

- restoration ({{Isaiah 11:6-9|Isaiah 11:6–9}}).

- LORD GOD (Hebrew *Yah Yahweh*): The first word (*Yah*) is a shorter form of the second (*Yahweh*). 

- *the LORD GOD is my strength and my song*: See {{Exodus 15:2|Exodus 15:2}}; {{Psalm 118:14|Psalm 118:14}}.
God's salvation is like a deep, endless source of water that gives life (see also {{Isaiah 41:18|Isaiah 41:18}}; {{Psalm 87:7|Psalm 87:7}}).
*Make His works known among the peoples*: The story of salvation should be shared with everyone, not just the people of Israel ({{Psalm 67:2|Psalms 67:2}}; {{Psalm 70:4|70:4}}; {{Psalm 98:2|98:2}}).

At the time of this prophecy, Assyria was the major power. Isaiah anticipated the rise of Babylon as an even crueler kingdom that would destroy Judah and Jerusalem ({{Isaiah 39:6-7|Isaiah 39:6–7}}; chapters {{Isaiah 46:1-47:15|46–47}}). 

The universal language in {{Isaiah 13:1-14:23|Isaiah 13:1–14:23}} suggests that Babylon symbolizes all wicked and arrogant nations, similar to "Babylon the Great" in the book of Revelation ({{Revelation 18:1-24|Revelation 18}}). So, while this description of Babylon's fall refers to the historic fall in 539 BC, it also applies to the final judgment against the ultimate kingdom of evil ({{Revelation 19:1-21|Revelation 19}}).

Isaiah spoke many messages from God about the people and leaders of other nations. These included Babylon, Assyria, the Philistines, Moab, Syria and its capital city Damascus.

They also included the northern kingdom, Cush, Egypt, Edom, Arabia and Tyre. Cush was a nation in Africa south of Egypt. The desert area west of Babylon was called Arabia.

The messages were warnings about things that were going to happen. Most of these things were terrible and would lead to those nations being destroyed. Talking about them caused the prophet fear, pain and deep sadness. It isn’t known if the people and leaders of these nations knew about Isaiah’s prophecies. But the people of the southern kingdom were made aware of them. This was one way that God taught his people about the nations around them.

The prophecies showed that God had authority and power over those nations. The prophecies showed that God’s people shouldn’t trust any of those nations to save them. None of those nations could save them from stronger nations like Assyria and Babylon. The messages showed God’s people that God would bring judgement against all nations. He would bring judgement against their leaders for being proud and causing others to suffer.

The prophecies also showed God’s people that God wanted those other nations to know him. He wanted those nations to be humble. He wanted them to recognise that he is the Lord who rules over all. He wanted them to worship him and to become a blessing to other people groups. Isaiah’s messages invited these nations to trust the God of Jacob’s people as their own God. The messages invited them to come to God for safety and protection. This was a lesson for Jerusalem and the southern kingdom to do the same.

This section contains prophecies of judgment against the nations. By including a prophecy against Judah and Jerusalem ({{Isaiah 22:1-25|Isaiah 22:1–25}}) in the midst of prophecies against the pagan nations, Isaiah emphasized that Israel’s identity as God’s people would not protect them from God’s punishment when they sinned as the other nations do.

- A signal flag or banner, visible from far away, was often placed on a bare hilltop as a call to battle. 

- God opposes Babylon as the symbolic representative of all evil kingdoms.

- Just as Assyria was a weapon of God's wrath ({{Isaiah 9:4|Isaiah 9:4}}; {{Isaiah 10:5|10:5}}, {{Isaiah 10:15|15}}), other nations act as the Lord’s weapons and carry out his will. The Medes and Persians conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

- God’s wrath shows his justice and his intent to restore order by destroying evildoers ({{Isaiah 10:25-26|Isaiah 10:25–26}}; see {{Lamentations 2:22|Lamentations 2:22}}; {{Ezekiel 7:19|Ezekiel 7:19}}).

When pronouncing judgment that is still in the future, the prophets sometimes spoke as though it had already arrived. This emphasized the urgency of turning back to God ({{Ezekiel 30:3|Ezekiel 30:3}}; {{Joel 1:15|Joel 1:15}}; {{Joel 3:14|3:14}}; {{Obadiah 15|Obadiah 1:15}}; {{Zephaniah 1:7|Zephaniah 1:7}}).

*writhe like a woman in labor*: The day of the Lord brings sudden and overpowering pain and fear for the wicked (see also {{Jeremiah 30:6|Jeremiah 30:6}}; {{Hosea 13:13|Hosea 13:13}}; {{Micah 4:9|Micah 4:9}}, {{Micah 4:10|10}}; {{Micah 5:3|5:3}}).

Cosmic upheaval and darkness are common images for the day of the Lord, a time of God’s judgment (see also {{Ezekiel 32:7-8|Ezekiel 32:7–8}}; {{Joel 2:10|Joel 2:10}}, {{Joel 2:31|31}}; {{Joel 3:15|3:15}}; {{Matthew 24:29|Matthew 24:29}}; {{Mark 13:24|Mark 13:24}}; {{Revelation 6:12-13|Revelation 6:12–13}}; {{Revelation 8:12|8:12}}; compare {{Isaiah 30:26|Isaiah 30:26}}).
Solomon’s imported gold came from Ophir ({{1 Kings 9:28|1 Kings 9:28}}).

*I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken from its place*: This language shows that God’s judgment will be powerful and world-changing. (see study note on Isaiah 5:25; see also {{Haggai 2:7|Haggai 2:7}}, {{Haggai 2:21|21}}; {{Hebrews 12:26-27|Hebrews 12:26–27}}; {{Revelation 16:17-18|Revelation 16:17–18}}; {{Revelation 18:21-22|18:21–22}}).
These terrible acts of war would happen to Babylon. Babylon was a cruel conquering power (see also {{Psalm 137:8-9|Psalm 137:8–9}}; {{Jeremiah 6:11-12|Jeremiah 6:11–12}}; {{Nahum 3:10|Nahum 3:10}}).

- The Lord is sovereign and controls history. He can influence kingdoms to carry out his will. 

- The Medes from northwestern Iran joined Persian King Cyrus to fight against Babylon in 539 BC.
This image of Babylon as a forever haunted ruin contrasts with its greatness at its height (see {{Daniel 4:29-30|Daniel 4:29–30}}).

*She will never be inhabited … from generation to generation*: In Scripture, Babylon often represents idolatry (worship of false gods), immorality, imperial power, and oppression. It stands for human pride and rebellion against God.

One day, it will come to a complete end (see {{Revelation 18:2|Revelation 18:2}}; {{Revelation 19:2|19:2}}).

- The Hebrew word translated as *mercy* uses the image of a mother's care for her child to show God's merciful love for his people (see also {{Isaiah 49:15|Isaiah 49:15}}; {{Isaiah 66:13|66:13}}). 

- God chose Israel as his special people when he called Abraham (see {{Isaiah 41:8|Isaiah 41:8}}; {{Genesis 12:1-3|Genesis 12:1–3}}). Although their status did not change during the exile in Babylon, they faced God's anger like any other wicked nation because they rejected him. 

- *settle them in their own land*: This promise began to be fulfilled in 538 BC (see {{Ezra 1:1-11|Ezra 1:1–11}}). 

- People from many nations would join Israel as the people of God (see also {{Isaiah 2:3-4|Isaiah 2:3–4}}; {{Isaiah 11:11-12|11:11–12}}; {{Isaiah 19:18-25|19:18–25}}; {{Isaiah 60:1-14|60:1–14}}).
This message for Israel separates two prophecies of judgment against Babylon ({{Isaiah 13:1-22|Isaiah 13}}; {{Isaiah 14:3-23|14:3–23}}).

- Just as Israel was subject to the Lord, the nations of the world would also submit to the Lord through Israel ({{Isaiah 45:14|Isaiah 45:14}}; {{Isaiah 49:7|49:7}}, {{Isaiah 49:23|23}}; {{Isaiah 60:12|60:12}}, {{Isaiah 60:14|14}}; {{Isaiah 66:23|66:23}}). 

- The oppressed nation of Israel will rule over its enemies and gain power and favor with God.

*The LORD gives … rest* (repose; {{Isaiah 28:12|Isaiah 28:12}}; see {{Deuteronomy 25:19|Deuteronomy 25:19}}; {{2 Samuel 7:11|2 Samuel 7:11}}) from the sorrow, fear, slavery, and chains that Israel experienced under foreign oppressors (see {{Isaiah 9:4|Isaiah 9:4}}).

This taunting song about the king of Babylon is written like a funeral song. It speaks as if the king has already died.

The song mocks him and announces his downfall (compare {{Revelation 18:1-24|Revelation 18}}).

A *song of contempt* is a mocking song. It makes fun of someone by comparing that person to something else.

In this case, the king of Babylon is compared to a dead man going down to the place of the dead. The song imagines him entering that realm in defeat.

- The land and people will be peaceful and calm because the oppression has ended and the king of Babylon has died. 

- All of creation will join in praise, able to sing again (see also {{Isaiah 42:11|Isaiah 42:11}}; {{Isaiah 44:23|44:23}}; compare {{Romans 8:22|Romans 8:22}}).

- The Babylonians viewed the place of the dead, called *Sheol* in Hebrew, as a place from which no one returns. 

- *rise from their thrones*: The thrones represent the Babylonian belief that the afterlife continues like the present life. It seems the other kings are honoring Babylon's great king, but the following verses reveal a different story.
*weak, as we are*: The Babylonian king had no power over anyone after death and could not leave Sheol. The Israelites will mock this great king who seemed strong on earth but had no weaknesses.

- Babylon's strength, power, and music from the harp ended, and its greatness was destroyed (see also {{Revelation 18:22|Revelation 18:22}}). 

- Maggots and worms represented death and decay ({{Isaiah 66:24|Isaiah 66:24}}).

- *fallen from heaven, O day star*: These words refer to a well-known Canaanite story. In that story, the god Helel rebelled against the god El, who was the chief god of the Canaanite people. Helel was cast down from heaven.

Isaiah uses this image to describe the fall of the king of Babylon. Some interpret the fall of the king of Babylon as symbolizing the fall of Satan (see {{Ezekiel 28:1-26|Ezekiel 28}}; {{Luke 10:18|Luke 10:18}}; {{Revelation 12:9|Revelation 12:9}}). However, there is little evidence that Isaiah meant this directly. He was speaking about the historical king of Babylon.

- *son of the dawn*: This refers to the morning star, which appears briefly at dawn and then disappears as the sun rises. In the Latin Vulgate, this term is translated *Lucifer*, which means “morning star.” In later Christian tradition, Lucifer became a name for Satan. However, the Hebrew text here does not clearly refer to Satan.

This verse refers to a Canaanite belief about the gods. The Canaanites believed that their chief god, El, ruled from Mount Zaphon. This mountain was in the north (see {{Psalm 48:2|Psalm 48:2}}; in the New Testament, similar language appears in {{Matthew 11:23|Matthew 11:23}}; {{Luke 10:15|Luke 10:15}}).

This is a restatement of{{Isaiah 14:9-11|14:9–11}}. The spirits in the place of the dead will be surprised and amazed that the Babylonian king, who ruled the world with his merciless might, has absolutely no power in death.
The absence of a proper burial was a sign of great shame and dishonor. Unlike other kings, the king of Babylon would be disgraced in judgment.

As another sign of disgrace, the king of Babylon would have no children to continue his legacy. Because of their father's sins, God considers individuals in relation to their families and people. Here, the Babylonian king's children shared responsibility for their father's actions (see also {{Deuteronomy 5:9-10|Deuteronomy 5:9–10}}).
Isaiah summarized the earlier taunt ({{Isaiah 14:3-21|Isaiah 14:3–21}}) with this prophecy, spoken in the first person. God declares that Babylon will be destroyed and left in ruins.
*I have planned … I have purposed*: No nation can stop or resist God's plans to judge Assyria or his plans overall. The prophets understood and shared God's plan so his people could respond properly.

This prophecy continues to declare judgment on Assyria (see {{Isaiah 10:1-34|Isaiah 10}}). Placing this prophecy after the judgment against Babylon suggests a close connection between Assyria and Babylon.
This prophecy told what would happen when Sennacherib attacked Hezekiah some years later in 701 BC (see {{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|Isaiah 36–37}}).
The Lord’s power over Assyria is just one example of his sovereignty over the whole earth.

- The king who attacked Philistia was probably Ahaz ({{Isaiah 14:28|Isaiah 14:28}}).

- *a viper*: This probably refers to one of the later Assyrian kings, either Sennacherib (701 BC), Esarhaddon (680 BC), or Ashurbanipal (668 BC).
The advancing army, probably Assyria, would stir up clouds of dust like smoke that were ominously visible in the north.

*The LORD has founded Zion*: God was fully willing and capable of defending Judah, and he did not want the kingdom to make alliances with nations such as the Philistines to protect themselves from the invading Assyrians.

- Moab was located east of the Dead Sea. It was an enemy of Judah. 

- *in a night!*: The destruction would be quick and final.
This message of judgment and sorrow was about Moab's fall. The many references to Moabite places show that Isaiah knew Moab well.
In the ancient Near East, people shaved or cut off their beards to show deep sorrow (see {{Jeremiah 48:37|Jeremiah 48:37}}).

- Heshbon was once the capital of Sihon ({{Numbers 21:23-26|Numbers 21:23–26}}). 

- Elealeh was near Heshbon. 

- Jahaz was located between Heshbon and the Arnon River (see {{Jeremiah 48:34|Jeremiah 48:34}}).

- *My heart cries out over Moab*: The prophet joined the mourning to show how much Moab suffered. 

- Zoar was in the southeastern part of the Dead Sea ({{Genesis 14:2|Genesis 14:2}}; {{Genesis 19:23|19:23}}).

- The exact location of the waters of Nimrim is unknown (see also {{Jeremiah 48:34|Jeremiah 48:34}}). 

- *dried up … withered … the vegetation*: For more on natural resources drying up as a form of judgment, see study note on Isaiah 24:4.
The exact locations of the Brook of the Willows, Eglaim, and Beer-elim are unknown.

- *Dimon *is a play on the Hebrew word for *blood* (*dam*). 

- *blood*: Many people from Moab had already died, but their punishment had just started.

- Moab was famous for its sheep (see {{2 Kings 3:4|2 Kings 3:4}}). The Moabites sent lambs as tribute to Judah, acknowledging Judah's control over Moab. 

- Sela (*the cliff*), a mysterious and distant location, was likely where the Moabites fled through the desert.
Moab is making a request to Judah for asylum (protection in another country).
*do not betray … be a refuge*: Moab's situation would become so desperate that they would ask for refuge in other countries.

- This prophecy of salvation spoke about the future of David’s royal line. It promised hope for the dynasty of David.

- Acts of oppression and destruction would come to an end. This would happen when the hostility of Moab stopped (see {{2 Kings 13:20|2 Kings 13:20}}).
God would establish one of David’s descendants as king (see also {{Isaiah 9:7|Isaiah 9:7}}; {{Isaiah 11:1-5|11:1–5}}, {{Isaiah 11:10-12|10–12}}).
The Moabites were too proud, angry, and boastful to humble themselves before God.
The response to Moab’s request for asylum ({{Isaiah 16:1-4|Isaiah 16:1–4}}).

- The vineyards at Sibmah were near the Moabite city of Heshbon. 

- Moab was like a lush vine spreading far and wide, but Israel's beautiful vine reached the ends of the earth ({{Isaiah 27:6|Isaiah 27:6}}). 

- The location of Jazer is unknown.

- The hilltops were sites for pagan shrines (see {{Isaiah 15:2|Isaiah 15:2}}). 

- No one will be able to save them, including the idols the Moabites called on for protection (see {{Isaiah 40:18-19|Isaiah 40:18–19}}; {{Isaiah 44:18-19|44:18–19}}).

- *In three years, as a hired worker counts the years* (see also {{Isaiah 21:16|Isaiah 21:16}}): A man who sold himself into servitude would calculate the remaining time down to the last day. This verse refers to unknown events. 

- The glory of Moab will be ended, probably because of the Assyrian conquest of Moab (late 700s BC). 

- *those who are left will be few and feeble*: Though reduced by war, the Moabites still existed during Nehemiah’s time ({{Nehemiah 13:23|Nehemiah 13:23}}).
Damascus, the leader of the alliance between Syria and Israel against Judah, fell when the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III invaded in 732 BC.

This section includes predictions of judgment against Damascus, Israel, Ethiopia, and Egypt. The scene shifts from the crisis in 734 BC (the alliance of Syria and Israel; see study note on Isaiah 7:1–25) to the Assyrian crisis in 701 BC (see {{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|Isaiah 36–37}}).

- The towns of Aroer were east of the Dead Sea (see {{2 Kings 10:32-33|2 Kings 10:32–33}}). 

- *they will be left to the flocks*: The city would serve no other purpose.
The strategic fortified towns of Israel were the pride of Israel, but they could not resist God’s purposes.

- *the splendor of Jacob will fade*: God will judge all human pride. 

- Israel, once strong, will become weak. The nation will waste away like a sick person.
The vision shifts from Damascus ({{Isaiah 17:1-3|Isaiah 17:1–3}}) to Israel's northern kingdom. Damascus and Israel were allies against Judah, but Assyria later destroyed both.
The Valley of Rephaim was a fertile area in Judah. However, it appeared barren after each harvest.
Although the God of Israel judged the wickedness of Israel, he was still its God.

- The people mentioned here are either Israelites or all of humanity. 

- *look … turn their eyes*: They will once more trust in the Lord.

Canaanites and then Israelites worshiped the fertility goddess Asherah in wooded areas or, in the absence of wooded areas, by using Asherah poles (see {{Isaiah 27:9|Isaiah 27:9}}; {{Isaiah 65:3|65:3}}; {{Micah 5:14|Micah 5:14}}).
The Hivites and Amorites were part of the original people living in Canaan. The Israelites were to destroy them when they conquered the land (see {{Deuteronomy 20:17|Deuteronomy 20:17}}).

- The Israelites combined their faith in the Lord with Baal worship. They turned away from the Lord, who is the only God and will not share devotion with idols. 

- The term *Rock* refers to the Lord's ability to provide refuge (see {{Isaiah 26:4|Isaiah 26:4}}; {{Isaiah 30:29|30:29}}; {{Psalm 18:2|Psalm 18:2}}, {{Psalm 18:46|46}}).
At times, the sea represents opposition to God (see {{Job 7:12|Job 7:12}}; {{Job 26:12|26:12}}; {{Psalm 46:3|Psalms 46:3}}; {{Psalm 93:3|93:3}}).
God was present with Judah during the crisis.
*He rebukes them*: The Lord rules over the nations, just as he rules over the sea ({{Psalm 65:7|Psalm 65:7}}).

*In the evening … Before morning*: Trouble may come at night, but it will not last long.

Even in frightening situations, Israel can trust the Lord. He is able to rescue his people quickly (see {{Isaiah 37:36-38|Isaiah 37:36–38}}).

Ethiopia was located to the south of Egypt. It marked the southern border of Egypt’s kingdom.

At that time, Egypt was ruled by an Ethiopian dynasty (a family line of kings). One of its rulers was Piankhi, also known as Piye.
Both the banner and ram's horn were used to organize and send signals to armies during battles (see {{Judges 3:27|Judges 3:27}}; {{Judges 6:34|6:34}}; {{2 Samuel 2:28|2 Samuel 2:28}}).
The Lord is untroubled by human activities. He watches quietly from his dwelling place and acts when he chooses (see {{Psalm 2:1-4|Psalm 2:1–4}}).
*the flower becomes a ripening grape*: Ethiopia had made every effort to form alliances to protect itself against Assyria, but its alliance with Judah would not help.

Conquered or weaker nations often had to pay tribute to a dominant king in the region (see {{Isaiah 16:1|Isiah 16:1}}; {{2 Kings 3:4-5|2 Kings 3:4–5}}). The Ethiopians brought gifts to honor the Lord for defeating the Assyrians (see also {{2 Chronicles 32:23|2 Chronicles 32:23}}).

- Riding on a swift cloud shows God's control and power over creation ({{Psalm 104:3|Psalm 104:3}}). He is coming to judge Judah's enemies (see {{Deuteronomy 33:26|Deuteronomy 33:26}}; {{Psalm 18:9-10|Psalms 18:9–10}}; {{Psalm 68:4|68:4}}; {{Psalm 97:2-3|97:2–3}}). 

- The idols of Egypt tremble because they are weak and powerless, unable to help (see {{Isaiah 40:18|Isaiah 40:18}}; {{Isaiah 45:16|45:16}}; {{Isaiah 46:1|46:1}}).
Egypt relied heavily on the Nile for food, fish, and industry. When the Lord struck the Nile, Egypt would face severe difficulties, and its gods would not be able to help.
Egypt experienced many civil wars that damaged the country. The nation's fragile unity was falling apart.
People called upon idols, spirits, mediums, and those who consult the spirits of the dead to try to prevent destruction (see {{Isaiah 8:19-22|Isaiah 8:19–22}}; {{Isaiah 47:12-13|47:12–13}}).
*harsh master*: In 671 BC, the Assyrian king Esarhaddon invaded Egypt and destroyed Memphis, the royal city. In 663 BC, Ashurbanipal attacked and destroyed Thebes (see {{Nahum 3:8-10|Nahum 3:8–10}}).

The Nile River was essential for Egypt's survival. Any change in its flooding pattern impacted the entire country. In ancient Egypt, people saw the Nile as a god. However, the true God could easily dry it up.
*The workers in flax … and the weavers of fine linen will turn pale*: The drought destroyed the flax crops. As a result, the linen industry could not continue.

- Zoan was the capital of Egypt, located in the Nile delta (see {{Numbers 13:22|Numbers 13:22}}). 

- *princes … wise counselors*: The king relied on the strategies and advice of wise men ({{Isaiah 19:12|Isaiah 19:12}}; see {{Genesis 41:39-40|Genesis 41:39–40}}). 

- The officials of Zoan were famous for their wise ancestors, and Egypt often boasted about them.
The prophet mocked the leaders and wise men of Egypt, who could not prevent the disaster.
*Where are your wise men now?*: Compare {{1 Corinthians 1:20|1 Corinthians 1:20}}.
Memphis was an ancient capital in Egypt located south of the Nile Delta. It was destroyed by Esarhaddon in 671 BC.

- *There is nothing Egypt can do*: No leader, idol, or human wisdom can stop God’s judgment.

- The head and the tail represented all of Egypt's leaders, from the most important to the least important (see {{Isaiah 9:14-15|Isaiah 9:14–15}}).
*The uplifted hand* (literally *waving the hand*) was a threatening gesture.

- *five cities in the land of Egypt*: This likely means "a number of cities" (see also {{Isaiah 17:6|Isaiah 17:6}}; {{Isaiah 30:17|30:17}}). 

- Jews living in Egypt after Jerusalem's destruction spoke Hebrew, referred to here as the language of Canaan. 

- Heliopolis was dedicated to Re, the sun god. When Judah resisted the Lord, Isaiah imagined the Egyptians following the Lord.

This altar or monument might refer to the temple built by Jews at Elephantine in Egypt around 500 BC. It could also refer to another Jewish place of worship or a memorial the Egyptians made to honor the Lord.
The new Egypt would receive a place in God’s purposes together with Assyria and Israel.

- The altar ({{Isaiah 19:19|Isaiah 19:19}}) would be a sign and a witness of the Egyptians’ religious connection with Israel (see {{Isaiah 19:24-25|19:24–25}}). 

- God answers the prayers of those who ask the Lord for help. 

- The Lord is a savior; he would protect the Egyptians just as he protected Jerusalem from the Assyrians.

- *strike Egypt*: The Hebrew verb here is the same as the one used for the tenth plague ({{Exodus 12:13|Exodus 12:13}}, {{Exodus 12:23|23}}, {{Exodus 12:27|27}}), reminding us of God's actions during the exodus. 

- The Lord, who sends a plague, can also heal. 

- *He will hear their prayers and heal them*: This expresses a covenantal relationship between the Lord and Egypt (see {{Isaiah 65:24|Isaiah 65:24}}).

- Traditionally, Egypt and Assyria were enemies of each other and of Israel. They were deeply involved in idol worship, but they would abandon their hostility and idols to worship the true God. 

- In the rugged terrain of the ancient Near East, a highway allowed for safe and easy travel and trade (see {{Isaiah 11:16|Isaiah 11:16}}; {{Isaiah 35:8|35:8}}; {{Isaiah 40:3|40:3}}; {{Isaiah 62:10|62:10}}).
Israel will be a blessing, fulfilling God's promise to Abraham ({{Genesis 12:3|Genesis 12:3}}).

Two titles usually meant for Israel, *My people* and *My handiwork* (see {{Isaiah 29:22|Isaiah 29:22}}; {{Isaiah 32:18|32:18}}), are used here for foreign nations. The Lord promised to consider those from other nations who turn to him as his special possession ({{Isaiah 63:17|Isaiah 63:17}}).

- Sargon of Assyria is Sargon II, who ruled from 721 to 705 BC. 

- Ashdod was one of the five Philistine cities that rebelled against Assyria in 713 BC.
Ashdod’s reliance on Egypt and Ethiopia was useless. As a complement to his words, Isaiah walked about exposed and barefoot, a symbolic action for what God would do.

- Prophets often wore sackcloth or other rough clothing to show mourning for the people's sins (see {{2 Kings 1:8|2 Kings 1:8}}; {{Mark 1:6|Mark 1:6}}). 

- *naked*: This means exposed in some way, possibly even completely nude.
This symbolic event happened about three years before Ashdod fell (see {{Isaiah 20:2|Isaiah 20:2}}). Through this event, Isaiah served as an example for the people (see {{Isaiah 8:18|Isaiah 8:18}}).
Philistia’s downfall was a warning to the people of Judah, who also relied on Egypt and other alliances rather than on God.
